scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a two-view response that leans toward preserving wilderness while granting that careful development is sometimes justified; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Wild forests, mountains, and rivers are among a nation's most precious treasures.
Some people believe a government should preserve its wilderness areas in their natural state, while others believe these areas should be developed for economic gain.
I lean toward preserving wilderness, but I accept that careful development is sometimes justified.
First, preserving wilderness in its natural state brings deep and lasting value.
Wild areas protect countless plants and animals and keep the natural balance healthy.
For example, untouched forests clean our air and water and shelter species found nowhere else.
This shows that wilderness provides benefits that no built development could ever replace.
Natural places also give people beauty, peace, and a connection to the living world.
Once a wilderness is destroyed, it can almost never be brought back.
For these reasons, I believe wilderness deserves strong protection.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why some development is justified

sentences.text: Second, however, the opposing view rightly notes that some development can be justified.
People need jobs, energy, and resources, and wild land sometimes holds what a society requires.
Consider a poor region where careful, limited development could lift many families out of poverty.
Such cases show that human needs cannot always be ignored for the sake of untouched land.
Responsible development that protects most of the wilderness can sometimes serve both people and nature.
Refusing all development could leave struggling communities without the means to survive.
Both views, then, hold part of the truth and must be weighed together.
In conclusion, I believe governments should generally preserve their wilderness areas.
But careful, limited development can be justified when human needs are truly pressing.
The wisest policy protects most wilderness while allowing responsible development where it is genuinely needed.
